blocks.content: Parliament may by law form a new State by separation of territory from any State or by uniting two or more States or parts of States or by uniting any territory to a part of any State.

rows: Admission or establishment of new states
Formation or reorganisation of existing states
Territories outside the existing Union of India
Territories already forming part of the Union of India
External admission of new units into India
Internal re-adjustment of boundaries, names, and areas

items: The views of the concerned State Legislature are NOT binding on the Parliament or the President.
A bill proposing changes under Article 3 requires ONLY a simple majority in Parliament.
Article 3 deals with internal reorganisation of existing Indian states, whereas Article 2 relates to admission or establishment of new states that were not part of India.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Article 3 authorizes Parliament to form new states, alter areas, boundaries, or names of existing states.
A bill under Article 3 can be introduced in either House of Parliament only on the prior recommendation of the President.
The President must refer the bill to the concerned state legislature to express its views within a specified time limit.
Parliament is not bound by the views of the state legislature and may accept or reject them entirely.
Changes made under Article 3 are passed by a simple majority and are not considered Constitutional Amendments under Article 368.
